summaries.example: Imagine your friend falls and scrapes a knee. You may notice the worried look on their face, feel a little of their sadness, and understand that they need help. If you feel sad because they are sad, while remembering that the sadness belongs to them, this is close to empathy. If everyone in a room starts laughing just because others are laughing, that is emotional contagion. If you feel worried for your friend and want them to be okay, that is sympathy.
summaries.summary: Empathy helps human beings connect with one another. The word can mean several related things: noticing what another person thinks, imagining their point of view, sharing some of their feeling, or responding to their situation. Philosophers and psychologists have not always used the word in the same way, so the entry carefully separates empathy from emotional contagion, sympathy, and personal distress. It also examines whether empathy is our main way of knowing other minds. Some views say we use ourselves as a model and imagine what another person is thinking. Other views say we directly perceive people as thinking and feeling beings through their expressions and actions. Empathy may support helping and moral life, but it is not automatically fair or accurate. We often respond more strongly to people who are nearby, familiar, or similar to us. Understanding another person also depends on culture, background, information, and our own past experiences. The entry presents these ideas as ongoing philosophical and psychological debates rather than as one final answer.
key_ideas: Empathy is a group of abilities, not just one feeling. It can involve understanding thoughts, sharing feelings, and caring about someone.
Empathy is different from emotional contagion, sympathy, and personal distress, even though these can happen together.
People disagree about how empathy works. Some think we partly recreate another person’s experience; others think we notice meaning directly in faces, voices, and actions.
Empathy can help friendship, cooperation, and kindness, but it can also favor people who seem close or familiar.
We cannot become exactly the other person. Listening, learning about their situation, and using imagination can improve our understanding.
summaries.why_it_matters: Empathy affects how we make friends, solve disagreements, care for others, and understand stories about people unlike us. Knowing its strengths and limits can help us listen more carefully. It can also remind us that feeling close to someone is not always the same as treating everyone fairly.

important_terms.definition: Trying to understand or share another person’s feelings or point of view while knowing that you are still yourself.
Catching another person’s emotion without clearly noticing that it came from them.
Feeling concern for someone who is having a hard time and wanting their well-being to improve.
The ability to tell that another person has thoughts and feelings that are different from your own.

questions_to_think_about: Can you understand someone’s sadness without becoming sad yourself?
When might caring about one person make it harder to treat everyone fairly?
What could you learn by listening to someone describe an experience you have never had?
Is copying someone’s expression the same as understanding their feeling?

summaries.example: Suppose a student is accused of cheating. One classmate imagines being in the student’s situation and tries to understand the fear, embarrassment, and reasons behind the student’s actions. That is perspective-taking, and it may include reenacting the student’s reasoning. Another classmate simply notices the student’s nervous expression and understands that the student is distressed; a phenomenological account may describe this as a direct perception of another minded person rather than an inference from analogy. A third classmate feels upset because the scene is uncomfortable, but is mainly focused on their own discomfort: that is personal distress, not necessarily sympathy or empathy.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry treats empathy as a broad and contested family of psychological and philosophical phenomena. It may involve affective sharing, imaginative perspective-taking, recognition of another person’s mental states, or concern for that person’s welfare. Because researchers define and measure it differently, claims about empathy must be evaluated carefully. A central issue is whether empathy gives us knowledge of other minds. Simulation theorists propose that we use ourselves as a model and reenact another person’s mental processes; other philosophers argue that we perceive people as minded, embodied agents without first inferring a hidden mind from physical behavior. Contemporary discussion of mirror neurons has revived inner-imitation accounts, although critics question whether neural resonance explains understanding or presupposes it. The entry also examines empathy’s role in interpreting history, literature, and social action. Empathy can help an interpreter grasp an agent’s reasons, but it cannot be the only method: cultural knowledge, evidence, language, and critical interpretation matter. Finally, empathy may support altruism, cooperation, and solidarity, yet it is vulnerable to in-group, proximity, salience, and similarity biases. The source therefore presents empathy as important but neither automatically accurate nor sufficient for moral judgment.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes emotional contagion, proper empathy, sympathy, and personal distress. Proper empathy requires some awareness that the experience is connected to another person rather than simply being one’s own.

Empathy is debated as an epistemic route to knowledge of other minds. Simulation theories emphasize imaginative reconstruction, while phenomenological approaches emphasize direct perception of embodied, expressive persons.

The traditional inference from analogy treats one’s own mind as directly known and other minds as inferred from behavior. Critics argue that this framework struggles to explain how mental concepts apply to others at all.

In the human sciences, empathy or reenactment may help explain an agent’s reasons, but historical and social understanding also requires language, cultural context, source criticism, and broader narratives.
Empathic understanding is perspectival and comes in degrees. Differences in experience, culture, values, and embodiment can limit what one can grasp from the inside.
Empathy may encourage helping and solidarity, but its partiality can distort moral judgment. Sympathy, reflection, principles of justice, and corrective viewpoints may be needed to regulate it.
summaries.why_it_matters: Empathy is involved in ordinary mindreading, relationships, education, historical interpretation, medicine, democratic discussion, and moral psychology. Understanding its different forms helps prevent category mistakes—for example, confusing personal distress with concern for another. It also clarifies why emotional closeness can motivate care while simultaneously producing unfair partiality. A mature account treats empathy as a useful, limited, and potentially regulable capacity rather than as a guaranteed moral guide.

important_terms.definition: A broad family of abilities involving awareness of another person’s mental life, imaginative perspective-taking, affective sharing, and related concern.
A view that we understand another person by using our own mental processes as a model and imaginatively recreating their thoughts or feelings.
The philosophical project of explaining how we understand beliefs, desires, emotions, intentions, and reasons in other people.
A proposed neural overlap between observing an action or expression and performing or experiencing something similar; its interpretation as a basis for empathy is disputed.
Concern for another person’s suffering or need from the observer’s standpoint, rather than sharing the person’s exact emotion.
A self-focused reaction to another person’s distress: the observer feels upset, alarmed, or troubled rather than primarily concerned for the other.
The position that understanding texts, actions, and historical events requires interpretive understanding and cannot be reduced to natural-scientific explanation.
The idea that empathy naturally favors the nearby, vivid, familiar, attractive, or in-group person, which can conflict with impartial fairness.

questions_to_think_about: Does imagining how you would feel in another person’s situation reveal their perspective, or mainly reveal your own?
Can mirror-neuron activity explain understanding, or might it depend on an understanding already in place?
Should the human sciences use a different method from the natural sciences? What would be gained or lost by that division?
If empathy favors vivid individuals over large groups, how should moral reasoning respond?
Can empathy contribute to morality without being the foundation or source of moral authority?

summaries.example: At lunch, Maya notices that Jordan is quiet after receiving a disappointing team result. Maya imagines how Jordan might be feeling and asks instead of guessing. If she begins to feel some of Jordan’s disappointment while remembering that it is Jordan’s experience, this resembles empathy. If she feels worried for Jordan and wants to help, that is sympathy. If the whole table becomes gloomy without knowing why, that is emotional contagion. If Maya becomes upset mainly because the awkward moment makes her uncomfortable, that is personal distress.
summaries.summary: Empathy is often described as understanding or sharing another person’s mental and emotional life, but the term covers several different abilities. A person may catch an emotion from a crowd, imagine another person’s viewpoint, share an emotion while recognizing it as the other person’s, feel concern for that person, or become upset mainly because the situation troubles them. The SEP entry explains why these differences matter. Philosophers have asked whether empathy is our main way of knowing other minds. One approach says we use our own minds as a model and simulate another person’s thoughts or feelings. Another approach says we directly perceive people as expressive, embodied beings rather than first seeing them as objects and then reasoning to a hidden mind. Research about mirror neurons has been used in support of simulation, though its meaning is debated. Empathy is also important in the human sciences, where understanding a person’s reasons may require imaginative reenactment. Still, no interpreter can simply become another person. Background, culture, values, and past experiences shape what can be understood. Empathy can encourage cooperation and helping, but it may favor familiar or nearby people and therefore conflict with justice. The entry presents empathy as valuable, complicated, and in need of reflection and correction.
key_ideas: The word empathy has been used in several ways, so philosophers and psychologists separate related experiences instead of treating them as identical.
Some accounts explain empathy as inner imitation or simulation. Other accounts say we directly recognize people as minded beings through their expressive bodies and actions.
Understanding people in history or society requires more than imagining their feelings. Cultural knowledge, evidence, language, and context also matter.
Empathy can make helping more likely, but it does not always produce fair behavior. Caring intensely about one person may lead us to overlook others.
Our experiences limit empathy, but we can improve understanding through listening, testimony, imagination, stories, and careful discussion.
The entry does not settle every disagreement. It shows why empathy is important while warning that it is not always accurate, impartial, or morally sufficient.
summaries.why_it_matters: Empathy shapes how we respond to classmates, family members, strangers, books, and public problems. Learning its different forms can make conversations more thoughtful: we can ask whether we are understanding someone, sharing a feeling, or merely reacting to our own discomfort. It also helps explain why good intentions are not enough; fair decisions may require evidence, principles, and attention to people who are less visible.

important_terms.definition: A set of abilities for recognizing, imagining, or sharing another person’s thoughts and feelings, often while keeping track of the difference between self and other.
When people pick up an emotion from those around them without needing to understand whose emotion it is or why it began.
Concern for another person’s suffering or needs, viewed from the standpoint of someone who cares about that person’s welfare.
Imagining another person’s situation or reasoning in order to understand their point of view.
The philosophical question of how we can know that other people have minds, feelings, beliefs, and desires.
A proposal that people understand others partly by running a version of another person’s mental process in their own minds.
A tendency for empathy to be stronger toward people who are close, familiar, vivid, similar, or part of one’s group.

questions_to_think_about: How is sympathy different from sharing another person’s feelings?
Why might a vivid story affect us more than information about many people?
Can someone understand an experience they have never had? What kinds of help would make that understanding better?
Why might historians need both empathy and evidence?
Should fairness sometimes correct what empathy makes us want to do?
